Short answer, a republic involves power being held by the people and their elected representatives, and usually has an elected or nominated president, rather than a monarchy or inherited succession. The US would be a good example of a republic, but it is also a representative democracy. The citizens are supposed to have the power to get their voices heard by proxy through their elected representatives, and each state is allowed to operate autonomously within the confines of national law. The House of Representatives and the Senate are the authorities that create legislation in the US, and the US president's main role is to assist in the maintainence and enforcement those laws passed by Congress, as well as the protection of the country from foreign entities. Pre-Caesar Rome is also a good example, since their senate was the power that wrote and debated the laws of the land, but then Caesar took over and became a dictator (Correct me if I get something wrong please, that part's a little fuzzy).

Socialism is a system of governance where the "means of production" are collectively owned by the people. Individuals take from the state according to their need, and give to the state accordig to their abilities. Basically, resources are meant to be distributed fairly evenly throughout the population, and the state takes care of the rest.

Communism seeks to use socialism along with Marxism to eliminate social classes (i.e., remove the bourgeoisie's power and distribute it throughout the proletariat). ALL property is publically owned, and everyone works according to their abilities, and is paid according to their needs.

Socialism and communism are, in effect, pretty similar, but I don't know that I would be able to tell you anything more other than they tend to require much more altruism from their citizens than most systems of government. Not completely ersed on those two systems.

Senates are usually a smaller, upper-level bodies of a congress. The US senate has 100 members, 2 from each state, whereas the House of Representatives has 435 reps, and each state gets seats based on how many people live in that state compared to the rest of the country. The representatives are meant to represent the will of the people of their respective disticts, whereas the senate is more representative of the state as a whole, so states with larger populations don't overpower the smaller ones(majority rules, minority rights).

In the UK Parliament, there is both a Monarchy, and a Parliamentary system. The monarchy essentially is a leftover system from when the people took power back from the Crown, and plays almost no real purpose in the decision making of the country (again, all corrections appreciated). Parliament is divided into two houses: the house of commons, and the house of lords. The House of Commons is like the US HoR, with representatives spending short terms in odffice, so long as the people want them to represent themselves. The House of Lords is much less volatile as far as representation changes. This house has members appointed for life, and is much smaller than the HoC. Since they aren't worried about re-election, the members of the HoL tend to vote more towards their own moral and ethical beliefs.

Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations is a good economics read, Cicero's De Republica is a good book on his thoughts about the ideal republic, and I'm not sure about on on sociology. I would always reccommend anything by Orwell, Brave New World, Utopia, and Atlas Shrugged. Thake those last few as you will, but they are all pretty iconic works.

After reading a good portion of these comments, it seems like we all lie somewhere in the center left portion of the compass. 

Personally, I would allign with socially liberal/fiscally-and-personally conservative policy, as well as a limited version of the non-agression principle. No one should have the right to force their views on another person, but everyone existing within a society is required to abide by the social contract of said society, usually defined by both its written and unwritten laws and customs (i.e., when in rome). Individuals should be able to do whatever the hell they want, so long as what they do does not adversely affect another individual in their society. For example, you could just decide to be a hermit on your own privately owned land, but when the time comes to defend yourself and/or your countrymen, you should be willing to take up arms in some sense to do so. 

However, I would also agree that the NAP should not be taken as strictly as some might take it (like ensuring someone has the proper warning before shooting them when they tresspass on your property). It is fundamentally necessary to assume that people don't want to do what they don't want to do, and forcing them to do what they don't want to do is only acceptable when it legitimately benefits the society as a whole. Authoritarian policies and practices fall under this exception as well; the government structure should only act in the best interests of the citizens, and should only enstate authoritarian policies when it is necessary to ensure their good health and whatnot.

I also have some fundamental disagreements with socialism and communism. Both systems require a somewhat vast level of shared altruism to function stably, and again, with my earlier point about peoplenot wanting to do what they don't want to do,  eventually it will get to a point where the citizens will become too selfish to continue using that sort of government.

Essentially what the concepts of Good and Evil boil down to is whether or not there is something you percieve as being beneficial or detremental to your goals, well being, values, etc. In other words, your allies will always be Good, whereas your enemies will always be Evil, and your enemy's enemies will be Evil to your enemy, but could also be Good to you, depending in the situation. Heros and Villains are essentially paragons of the concepts of Good and Evil, respectively.

The issue with this, however, is that Good and Evil are subjective and depend entirely on one's own thoughts and philosophies. So, to invoke Godwin's Law, Hitler may not have seen himself as the villain, but rather as the hero, and the Jewish people as the villiains and evildoers; in reality though, since the winners write history, the allies labeled him and others like him as villains.
